surface_forms: Mon cousin le prince de Guermantes

appraisal_events.evidence: Mme Verdurin presses Morel to break with « un personnage flétri, qui n'est reçu nulle part », claims « la police l'a à l'œil », that Charlus is « entièrement ruiné » and calls Morel « la fable du Conservatoire » — while the narrator notes she forgets « qu'elle le recevait presque chaque jour » and that her assertions are « diaboliquement utiles, sinon rigoureusement exactes ».
appraisal_events.explanation: Mme Verdurin mounts a sustained, largely mendacious campaign of defamation that succeeds in detaching Morel from Charlus; the narrator reports her triumph while explicitly exposing the lies and the melodramatic appetite that drive it.

appraisal_events.evidence: Publicly repulsed by Morel (« Laissez-moi, je vous défends de m'approcher »), the feared orator is left « muet, stupéfait », in « une paralysie de tous les membres et de la langue », able only to stammer « Qu'est-ce que cela veut dire, qu'est-ce qu'il y a ? », the Verdurins looking away; the narrator glosses him as « un vrai impulsif, mais un faux brave » repeating the ancient pantomime of « l'épouvante des nymphes poursuivies par le Dieu Pan ».
appraisal_events.explanation: The passage culminates in Charlus's public collapse before an assembled salon, and the narrator's own commentary — false brave, grand seigneur whose superiority proves inessential, terrified nymph — makes the diminishment authorial rather than merely reported.

status_effects.explanation: He is defamed behind his back, publicly repudiated by his protégé, and abandoned by his hosts in front of the whole salon; nobody comes to his aid.
The man whose rages once made a room tremble is struck dumb and reduced to pleading, interrogative glances, losing all leverage at the moment he expected triumph.
She dominates the scene entirely through speech: she wins Morel over, secures her Wednesdays, and is « inondée de la joie » of a victory she engineered word by word.
The narrator undercuts the victory by exposing her as drunk on melodrama, lying without checking herself, and unable to hold back the damaging word that burns her tongue.

Although he lands the public blow, the passage stages him as a credulous dupe sweating and weeping on cue, hunting « une dignité d'emprunt pour couvrir la sienne en lambeaux », with the valet's-son origin circulating around him.

ambiguities: Mme Verdurin's movement is genuinely two-sided: the passage plainly awards her the local victory, but its narration is organized around exposing her calumnies, so her gain is registered rhetorically while her general appraisal falls.
